title: 139. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Time-Distance-Speed Word Problems
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Speed as Distance Divided by Time
questions.learningObjective: Calculate speed from given distance and time.
questions.question: A car travels \(150\text{ km}\) in \(3\text{ h}\). What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Average speed is total distance divided by total time: \(\frac{150}{3}=50\text{ km/h}\). The alternative \(450\) multiplies distance by time, producing incompatible dimensions.
questions.hint: Identify the total distance and the relevant travel time.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate distance from speed and time.
questions.question: A train travels at \(60\text{ km/h}\) for \(3\text{ h}\). How far does it travel?
questions.explanation: Distance equals speed multiplied by time: \(60\times 3=180\text{ km}\). The alternative divides speed by time, \(\frac{60}{3}=20\), rather than multiplying; its calculation does not have distance units.
questions.hint: Check which operation on speed and time leaves a unit of distance.

questions.concept: Time as Distance Divided by Speed
questions.learningObjective: Calculate time from distance and speed.
questions.question: A bus covers \(240\text{ km}\) at a constant speed of \(80\text{ km/h}\). How long does the journey take?
questions.explanation: Time is distance divided by speed: \(\frac{240}{80}=3\text{ h}\). The alternative reverses the ratio, \(\frac{80}{240}=\frac{1}{3}\), instead of dividing distance by speed.
questions.hint: Rearrange the distance-speed-time relation to isolate the time.

questions.concept: Time to Meet for Opposite-Direction Motion
questions.learningObjective: Determine meeting time for two objects moving toward each other.
questions.question: Two towns are \(300\text{ km}\) apart. Two cars start at the same time from the two towns and travel toward each other at \(60\text{ km/h}\) and \(40\text{ km/h}\). How long will it take for them to meet?
questions.explanation: The cars approach at combined speed \(60+40=100\text{ km/h}\), so they meet after \(\frac{300}{100}=3\text{ h}\). The alternative subtracts the approaching speeds, \(\frac{300}{60-40}=15\text{ h}\), instead of adding them.
questions.hint: Identify the total distance and the relevant travel time.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate average speed for a round trip over equal distances.
questions.question: A car travels from town A to town B at \(30\text{ km/h}\) and returns along the same road at \(60\text{ km/h}\). What is its average speed for the whole trip?
questions.explanation: Let the one-way distance be \(d\). Total distance is \(2d\). Total time is \(\frac{d}{30}+\frac{d}{60}=\frac{3d}{60}=\frac{d}{20}\). Therefore, average speed is \(\frac{2d}{\frac{d}{20}}=40\text{ km/h}\). Option B is the arithmetic mean of the two speeds, which does not apply to equal distances.
questions.hint: Let the one-way distance be \(d\) and compare the total distance with the total time.

questions.learningObjective: Determine time for a faster object to catch a slower object with a head start.
questions.question: A cyclist leaves a point at \(08{:}00\) traveling at \(40\text{ km/h}\). A motorcyclist leaves the same point at \(10{:}00\) traveling at \(60\text{ km/h}\) along the same road. How long after the motorcyclist starts will the motorcyclist catch the cyclist?
questions.explanation: By \(10{:}00\), the cyclist has traveled \(2\times 40=80\text{ km}\). The relative speed is \(60-40=20\text{ km/h}\). The time to close the \(80\text{ km}\) gap is \(\frac{80}{20}=4\text{ h}\) after the motorcyclist starts. Therefore, the motorcyclist catches the cyclist after \(4\text{ h}\). The alternative includes the cyclist's two-hour head start and reports \(6\text{ h}\) from the earlier departure, not \(4\text{ h}\) from the motorcyclist's start.
questions.hint: Find the cyclist's head-start distance, then track the rate at which the gap closes.

questions.concept: Time to Pass a Fixed Point
questions.learningObjective: Calculate time for a train to pass a fixed point.
questions.question: A train \(200\text{ m}\) long travels at \(20\text{ m/s}\). How long does it take to pass a fixed pole?
questions.explanation: To pass a fixed pole, the train travels a distance equal to its own length, \(200\text{ m}\). The time is \(\frac{200}{20}=10\text{ s}\). Therefore, the train takes \(10\text{ s}\) to pass the pole. The alternative doubles the train length, as if the pole were another equally long train.
questions.hint: Identify the total distance and the relevant travel time.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate time for a train to completely cross a bridge.
questions.question: A train \(300\text{ m}\) long travels at \(30\text{ m/s}\). How long does it take to completely cross a bridge \(600\text{ m}\) long?
questions.explanation: To completely cross the bridge, the train must cover its own length plus the bridge length. The total distance is \(300+600=900\text{ m}\). The time is \(\frac{900}{30}=30\text{ s}\). Therefore, the train takes \(30\text{ s}\). Option B ignores the train's length.
questions.hint: Check what distance the front of the train must cover before the whole train has left the bridge.

questions.concept: Meeting Time on a Circular Track
questions.learningObjective: Determine meeting time for two objects moving in opposite directions around a circular track.
questions.question: Two runners start from the same point on a \(400\text{ m}\) circular track at the same time and run in opposite directions at \(5\text{ m/s}\) and \(3\text{ m/s}\). How long until they meet again?
questions.explanation: Because the runners move in opposite directions, their speeds add. The combined speed is \(5+3=8\text{ m/s}\). They meet again after together covering one full lap, so the time is \(\frac{400}{8}=50\text{ s}\). Therefore, they meet again after \(50\text{ s}\). The alternative ignores the second runner, using \(\frac{400}{5}=80\text{ s}\) instead of the relative speed.
questions.hint: Track the rate at which the runners together cover one full lap.

questions.concept: Average Speed for a Two-Stage Journey
questions.learningObjective: Calculate average speed for a journey with two stages.
questions.question: A cyclist travels \(30\text{ km}\) at \(15\text{ km/h}\) and then \(60\text{ km}\) at \(20\text{ km/h}\). What is the average speed for the entire journey?
questions.explanation: The leg times are \(\frac{30}{15}=2\text{ h}\) and \(\frac{60}{20}=3\text{ h}\). The average speed is \(\frac{30+60}{2+3}=18\text{ km/h}\). The alternative \(17.5\text{ km/h}\) is the arithmetic mean of the two speeds, which would require equal travel times.
questions.hint: Identify the total distance and the relevant travel time.
